subtype: Approach: copying the previous lead's style without fit [Pitfall]
passage:
Kunal: Tell me about the stand-ups.

Jahnavi: My old boss ran a forty-minute stand-up every morning and a tracker that showed everyone's hours. It worked, for a department of thirty senior people. So when I became lead of six of us, all around twenty-five, I copied it. Long daily stand-ups, a strict tracker, updates due by five. Within a fortnight people stopped joking. Updates got short and careful. Nobody raised problems, because everything was being counted. One afternoon a teammate asked, "Are you checking up on us?" and I heard how quiet the room had become. That system suited my boss's group. It didn't suit this one, and I hadn't asked whether it would.

qa.q: How long were the stand-ups run by Jahnavi's old boss?
qa.a: The old boss ran a forty-minute stand-up every morning.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel on hearing the teammate ask whether the team was being checked up on?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt shaken and a little ashamed, suddenly hearing how quiet and watched the room had become.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try to fit the style to this team, and why?
qa.a: Jahnavi could ask the team what kind of updates help them and shorten the stand-ups, because a routine works better when the people using it helped shape it.

qa.q: How did the team experience the new routine?
qa.a: The team felt policed and cautious, so they stopped joking and raised no problems.

grounding: Illustrates a new lead copying an old boss's daily long stand-ups and strict tracking with a young team that feels policed and goes quiet.

subtype: Approach: hiding struggles to look capable [Pitfall]
passage: Naveen, I'll tell you about my first project as lead. I'm Kashish. I was twenty-five, a young man scared of looking weak. So every Friday my report was green. Green, green, green, for a month. Meanwhile the modules from two teams refused to talk to each other, and I stayed silent, hoping to fix it myself over weekends. I never asked my manager for help, because I thought asking meant I couldn't lead. Then, five days before release, the integration test failed on every path. My manager looked at four weeks of green reports and asked how this could be. I had no answer except the truth. We shipped late, and for a long while my reports were read with a raised eyebrow.

qa.q: How long did Kashish report everything as green?
qa.a: Kashish reported green, green, green for a month.

qa.q: Why did Kashish not ask the manager for help?
qa.a: Kashish was scared of looking weak and believed asking for help meant not being able to lead.

qa.q: What could Kashish have done at the first sign of trouble, and why?
qa.a: Kashish could have told the manager about the two modules early and asked for help, because a problem shared in the first week is much cheaper to fix than one found five days before release.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt on seeing the failed test after four weeks of green reports?
qa.a: The manager was probably surprised and let down, having trusted reports that showed no trouble at all.

grounding: Illustrates a first-time lead reporting everything as fine for a month, never asking for help, so integration trouble surfaces only days before release.

subtype: Approach: admitting overload and re-scoping with the manager [Revision]
passage:
Wednesday. Two sprints behind, and I've been pretending otherwise for weeks. Last night I stopped. Made a one-page list: done (login, search, profile), at risk (payments, notifications), can be cut (dark mode, the export button). Took it to Lalit at ten this morning. My hands were sweating. Lalit read it twice, asked two questions, and said, "Thanks for telling me now, not later." Dark mode and the export button move to phase two. At stand-up afterwards the room felt different. Rohan actually smiled. Admitting it felt like failing for about ten minutes, and then it felt like the first proper plan I've made.

Preeti

qa.q: What did the list say could be cut?
qa.a: The list said dark mode and the export button could be cut.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel while handing the list to Lalit?
qa.a: Preeti felt nervous, with sweating hands, and expected it to feel like failing.

qa.q: What else could Preeti do to keep the team on track, and why?
qa.a: Preeti could update the same one-page list each week and share it with Lalit, because small regular updates stop a team from falling behind unseen.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt on receiving the list?
qa.a: Lalit was probably relieved and appreciative, glad to hear early exactly what was done and what was at risk.

grounding: Illustrates admitting being behind and bringing the manager a clear list of what is done, at risk and cuttable, so features move to phase two.

subtype: Approach: short retrospective and adaptive replanning [Revision]
passage:
Friday. Second retro since I set the same-day review rule. Sticky notes on the glass wall again: green for what worked, pink for what didn't. Two weeks ago there were nine pink notes, and almost all of them said the same thing: code reviews sitting for days. Sarita counted, and the average wait had been three days. I'd been one of the slow reviewers too. So the rule was simple: every review gets a first reply the same day, even if it's only "I'll look properly tomorrow morning." Today there are three pink notes. Reviews now wait less than a day, and the team closed more tickets this fortnight than in any before it. I felt a bit proud, and a bit relieved.

Aadhya

qa.q: How many pink notes were on the wall at this retro?
qa.a: There were three pink notes at this retro.

qa.q: How does Aadhya feel about how the review rule has worked?
qa.a: Aadhya feels a little proud and relieved that the rule has helped the team.

qa.q: What else could the team try to keep improving, and why?
qa.a: The team could rotate a review buddy each week, because sharing the job stops reviews from piling up on one or two people.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the changes?
qa.a: Sarita, who counted the waiting time, probably feels satisfied to see that count lead to a visible improvement.

grounding: Illustrates a fortnightly retrospective where a lead notices slow code reviews, sets a same-day review rule and sees the team's pace improve.

subtype: Approach: critical path thinking about dependent tasks [Thinking]
passage: I'm Imran, on the web team. In the second week I noticed Kiran at the whiteboard with a tangle of arrows between tasks. The mobile screens depended on the API. So did our web pages. Kiran drew the longest chain in red: API contract, then mobile and web side by side, then integration, then release. "If the contract slips, everything behind it slips," Kiran said, and booked a two-hour session with both teams that week. We argued over field names, dates and error messages, and by Friday the contract was written down and shared. Mobile and web started work on the same Monday. I can't tell whether Kiran had done this before. It only looked obvious afterwards.

qa.q: What did Kiran book with both teams that week?
qa.a: Kiran booked a two-hour session with both teams.

qa.q: What was Kiran probably worried about when drawing the red chain?
qa.a: Kiran was probably worried that a slipped contract would hold up everything behind it.

qa.q: What else could Kiran do to protect the plan, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could make sure nobody changes the contract without telling both teams, because a quiet change could break the work already started.

qa.q: How might the mobile team have seen the early session?
qa.a: The mobile team probably felt relieved that their work would not be stuck waiting, since the contract was settled before either team began building.

grounding: Illustrates a lead seeing that one contract blocks two teams and settling it early with both, so the longest chain of dependent tasks is not delayed.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: breaking work into estimated pieces to test feasibility [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Payments feature, timeline

Hi Darshan,

Thanks for the two-week request. Before I say yes or no, I broke the work into pieces and estimated the hours for each:

- connecting to the payment provider: 40
- transaction screens: 60
- refunds and failures: 50
- testing: 70
- security review: 20
- documentation and release: 20

That comes to 260 hours. With the two of us on it, that's about six weeks, not two. I've attached the sheet so you can check my numbers. I'd like to make this work, so I'm happy to go through it together and see what could shrink.

Neelam

qa.q: How many hours did the estimate total?
qa.a: That comes to 260 hours.

qa.q: What does Neelam feel about the two-week request?
qa.a: Neelam wants to make it work but is worried about promising something the numbers cannot support.

qa.q: What else could Neelam offer Darshan, and why?
qa.a: Neelam could offer a smaller first version that fits two weeks, because a choice of options is easier to accept than a plain refusal.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Neelam's email?
qa.a: Darshan may be surprised or worried about the date, but the attached sheet gives something concrete to discuss rather than an argument about feelings.

grounding: Illustrates a developer told to deliver in two weeks listing every task with hours and finding it needs about six weeks, giving a factual basis.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: offering scope options instead of a flat no [Action]
passage:
Note for my file, engineering manager. On Monday I asked Nitya for the whole payments feature in two weeks. Nitya did not say no. On Tuesday Nitya came with a one-page sheet holding three options: A, the whole feature over six weeks; B, the main payment path in two weeks, with settlement checked by hand each day; C, a two-week prototype that real customers would not use. Each option had a line on what it cost and what it risked. I asked which Nitya recommended. B, with reasons. I chose B and told the sales team. Then I took two other tasks off Nitya's plate and booked the daily manual check with the finance team.

Vikas

qa.q: Which option did the manager choose?
qa.a: The manager chose option B, the main payment path in two weeks with settlement checked by hand each day.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt on seeing three options instead of a plain no?
qa.a: Vikas was probably relieved and impressed, since the options turned a refusal into a decision Vikas could make.

qa.q: What else could Nitya do to help the manager decide, and why?
qa.a: Nitya could state a clear recommendation with reasons, as Nitya did, because a recommendation saves the manager from guessing which option is safest.

qa.q: How might Nitya have felt when the manager chose option B?
qa.a: Nitya probably felt heard and relieved, since the choice fit what Nitya recommended and came with two tasks removed.

grounding: Illustrates bringing a manager three scope options, a full build, a core flow with manual checking and a prototype, instead of a flat no.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: prioritising by urgent versus important [Thinking]
passage: The date on the calendar had not moved: launch was in nine days. Aparna gathered the five of them around a table in the Pune office and asked one question. "What does a customer absolutely have to have at launch, and what is only nice to have?" Ganga, from support, said customers write in about failed logins and payments, never about reports. The team sorted sticky notes into two columns. Login, payment and order confirmation went on the left. Reports, export and profile themes went on the right. "If everything is urgent, nothing gets protected," Aparna said aloud. They pinned the list up and told the manager the reports would follow in a second release. It felt like a loss for a moment, and then like a relief.

qa.q: Which parts went in the left column?
qa.a: Login, payment and order confirmation went on the left.

qa.q: How did the team feel about postponing reports and export?
qa.a: It felt like a loss for a moment and then like a relief, since the important parts were now protected.

qa.q: What else could the team do after launch, and why?
qa.a: The team could ask early customers which postponed feature matters most, because real requests show what to build first in the second release.

qa.q: How might Ganga in support see the decision?
qa.a: Ganga probably felt heard as the voice of customers, since the failures customers write about were exactly what got protected.

grounding: Illustrates a team facing a tight date asking which parts customers need on day one and postponing reports and export while login and payment are protected.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: accepting silently and working nights [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Sunaina, and I sit two desks from Omkar. When the manager asked for the feature by the end of the month, Omkar said "Sure" without opening the estimate sheet. After that Omkar was still at the desk when the cleaners arrived, and at midnight the chat status still glowed green. The testing part was quietly dropped. Two weeks later the release shipped, and by Monday three bugs were live and customers were writing in. At the review the manager said, "Good, so that timeline works. Let's keep this pace next time." Omkar nodded, dark circles under the eyes. I don't know why Omkar said yes without asking. But nobody outside our corner knew what it had cost.

qa.q: How many bugs were live by Monday?
qa.a: Three bugs were live by Monday.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling while nodding at the review?
qa.a: Omkar was probably exhausted and reluctant to admit the strain, judging by the dark circles under the eyes.

qa.q: What could Omkar do before answering the next deadline request, and why?
qa.a: Omkar could check the estimate first and say what fits, because a yes that ignores the numbers hides the real cost from the manager.

qa.q: How might the manager see the result of the release?
qa.a: The manager saw a feature delivered on time and so assumed the timeline was reasonable, without knowing about the late nights and dropped testing.

grounding: Illustrates a junior lead accepting a deadline in silence and working nights, so quality drops and the manager concludes the date was reasonable.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: planning fallacy from optimistic guessing [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. The manager asked how long the checkout module would take. Urmila wanted to please, and pictured everything going smoothly. "Six days," she said. No time for testing, none for reviews. Zainab looked up from the next desk but said nothing.

Day 5. The code review sat in a queue for two days, and the test environment crashed and took another day to repair.

Day 9. Zainab began her planned leave, and her part, a payment helper, had not been handed over.

Day 19. The module was finally delivered, thirteen days after the promise. The manager, who had told the client "Friday", had to write an apology.

qa.q: How many days did Urmila promise for the module?
qa.a: Urmila said six days.

qa.q: What did Urmila want when giving the estimate?
qa.a: Urmila wanted to please the manager, and pictured everything going smoothly.

qa.q: What could Urmila do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Urmila could estimate each piece separately and add time for testing, reviews and colleagues' leave, because the best-case picture leaves no room for the usual delays.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt when writing the apology to the client?
qa.a: The manager probably felt embarrassed and let down, having promised the client a Friday on an estimate that had no slack.

grounding: Illustrates a developer wanting to please and giving a best-case estimate with no testing time, so reviews, environment problems and leave push delivery past the promise.
